#!/bin/bash
# build one C# file the way the lessons do (inside the image's restored project), and run it
rm -rf /tmp/cs && cp -r /opt/templates/csharp /tmp/cs && cp "$1" /tmp/cs/Program.cs
cd /tmp/cs
if ! out=$(dotnet build --no-restore -v q -nologo -clp:NoSummary 2>&1); then
  echo "$out" | grep ' error ' | sed -e 's# \[/tmp/cs/[^]]*\]##' -e 's#/tmp/cs/##' | sort -u
  exit 1
fi
dotnet bin/Debug/net10.0/Program.dll

langs.py/fetch.py:
import asyncio


async def fetch(name, ms):
    try:
        await asyncio.sleep(ms / 1000)
    except asyncio.CancelledError:
        print(f"({name} was cancelled)")
        raise
    return f"{name} done after {ms}ms"


async def main():
    users = asyncio.create_task(fetch("users", 30))
    orders = asyncio.create_task(fetch("orders", 10))
    print(await users)
    print(await orders)

    left, right = await asyncio.gather(fetch("left", 20), fetch("right", 20))
    print(left, "/", right)

    try:
        print(await asyncio.wait_for(fetch("slow", 500), timeout=0.05))
    except TimeoutError:
        print("slow call timed out")


asyncio.run(main())

go-lock-cs.out: Program.cs(10,9): error CS1996: Cannot await in the body of a lock statement

gotcha.title: Holding a lock across an `.await`
gotcha.looks_fine: Taking a lock, waiting, then changing the data and unlocking is ordinary code. Go's `sync` docs even say a locked `Mutex` "is not associated with a particular goroutine".
gotcha.rust_sees: `tokio::spawn` asks for a future that is `Send`, because the default runtime can resume a task on a different worker thread after any `.await`. The guard from a standard `Mutex` is not `Send`: the standard library docs say that on platforms that use POSIX threads a lock must be released on the thread that acquired it, so the guard may not travel with the task.
gotcha.why: The Tokio docs say it is "ok and often preferred" to use the standard `Mutex` in async code. The rule is to drop the guard before the next `.await`: lock, change and unlock in one statement, as the fix does. If the lock has to stay held across an `.await` (the docs' example is a database connection), use `tokio::sync::Mutex`, whose guard is designed for it. The compiler is not the only protection you need: the section above shows the same mistake, without `spawn`, compiling and then hanging, so for the one-thread case it is a real Rust bug and not only a rule.

fixed.name: src/main.rs

go.says: Go compiles and runs this. A `sync.Mutex` is not tied to a goroutine or a thread (the sync docs), so holding it while the goroutine sleeps is allowed.

csharp.says: C# rejects an `await` inside a `lock` statement. The C# docs say "You can't use the await expression in the body of a lock statement."
